title: Feedback that changes behaviour

audience.who: corporate employees who give feedback to peers or reports, in regular one-to-ones and reviews
audience.knows: giving feedback feels awkward and sometimes nothing changes afterwards
audience.cares_about: the other person actually doing something differently next time, without a tense conversation

outcome: After their next piece of feedback, the viewer names the specific behaviour and its impact, then asks a question instead of handing down a verdict, so the other person knows exactly what to change
through_line: Feedback changes behaviour when it describes a specific action and its impact and ends in a question; feedback that judges the person or stays vague only changes how they feel

arc_plan.what: A colleague gets told 'you need to communicate better' after a confusing status update; next week's update is just as confusing, because nothing told them what to repeat or stop. Framed as invented.
Name what the viewer will leave able to do: turn a vague verdict into feedback that names a specific behaviour, its impact, and ends in a question
The three-part shape, in order: the specific behaviour (not the person), its concrete impact, then a question that invites the other person's view and agrees what happens next
Two feedback lines on the same moment, one judging the person, one naming the behaviour and impact; the viewer picks which is likely to change next week's update
Back to the opening colleague: the same kind of update, now given feedback with the three-part shape; the question lands and the next update is clearer

must_cover.what: the three-part shape in order: specific behaviour, its impact, then a question
feedback aimed at the behaviour, not the person's character
why vague or person-directed feedback tends not to change what someone does next
the closing question is what turns the feedback into a conversation rather than a verdict
the method presented as common workplace practice, never as a named research finding unless the knowledge sheet grounds a specific attributable source

must_avoid: statistics or research citations unless the knowledge sheet grounds them with a real, named source
learning-styles or other debunked pop-psychology claims
invented lines attributed to a real study or person, presented as real
a tour of generic feedback tips instead of the one running example
"in this video we will" or any agenda slide
a trivia question in place of a real decision the viewer could face
the opening colleague made to look incompetent or embarrassed; the mistake is ordinary
HR, disciplinary or formal performance-review process detail
a real company or named real person
example_posture: One invented, ordinary workplace moment (an unclear status update or handoff), framed as illustrative and returned to twice, broken then fixed; generic colleagues, no real company, no industry jargon
visual_direction: A presenter figure to open with the hook and promise, and to close; inside, the one running workplace moment replayed twice between two illustrated colleagues, with the specific behaviour and its impact called out as they happen; the three-part shape held as a short on-screen sequence that returns unchanged at the check and payoff; a clear before-and-after contrast between the vague verdict and the specific ask
voice_note: A mentor who has given plenty of feedback that did not land before finding the shape; plain, warm, direct, never lecturing; say each point once
open_questions: No source document was supplied; must_cover relies on the knowledge sheet's general grounding of a recognised workplace feedback practice (behaviour, impact, question), not a company-specific source
2 minutes is tight for a full teaching arc; bridge and apply are dropped so hook, promise, one build section, check and payoff fit
